title: The Al and the Shepherd's Fire
summary: A band of shepherds on the high pastures of Ararat discover that the darkness between their campfires is not empty, and that the Al watches from the space between flames.
full_text:
In the time before the Flood, when the sons of Aram tended their flocks upon Ararat, there lived a shepherd named Torgom who feared nothing. He had wrestled wolves with his bare hands and once drove a leopard from his fold with a burning brand.

But the old women whispered of the Al, and Torgom laughed at them. 'What is an Al?' he asked. 'A shadow that mothers invent to keep children from wandering.' The old women crossed themselves and said nothing.

One autumn evening, when frost silvered the high meadows, Torgom drove his flock to a hollow beneath a basalt outcropping. He built three fires in a ring and settled in to watch the night. The other shepherds slept, but Torgom kept the first vigil.

In the second hour past midnight he noticed the cold. Not the mountain's natural cold, but a cold that crept between the fires like water through cracked earth. The flames did not dim, yet the warmth fled. Torgom peered into the space between the fires.

There, where the light should have met, was a patch of darkness that did not belong. It was not merely the absence of light but a darkness with weight and substance. And within it, two eyes opened.

They burned with a cold, wet light, like marsh-fire in still water, regarding him with ancient intelligence and utter mercylessness. The Al had come.

Torgom reached for his knife, but his hand would not obey him. The Al drifted closer, tall and thin, wrapped in hair like riverweed, its mouth a wound smiling. 'You laugh at the old women,' it whispered, its voice the sound of embers collapsing. 'But they know what you do not. I am the space between every flame. Every fire you build only makes more darkness for me.'

Torgom spoke from desperation, and desperation has its own wisdom. 'Then I will sit in the dark and face you without light.' The Al laughed. 'Fool. If you build no fire, I will come as the cold.'

Yet in the forest beyond, Torgom found something the Al had not predicted. The trees groaned in a wind he could not feel, and in their groaning was a sound that predated fire, predated light, predated even the darkness the Al called home. It was the voice of the earth itself, humming where neither fire nor shadow could reach.

At dawn Torgom told the shepherds to descend to the valley, to the rivers, to places where water spoke louder than shadow. Before leaving, he poured river water over the basalt and prayed to the spirits of the deep earth to hold the Al beneath the rock.

From that day the Armenians honored both fire and water, learning that the Al cannot be defeated by flame, for it feeds upon the shadows flame creates. But it is held at bay by running water, which speaks in a voice older than darkness, and by the deep roots of trees that remember the world before the Al first opened its eyes.
moral: Disbelief does not protect against what is real; only wisdom and respect for the old ways can hold darkness at bay.

title: Shir the Holy Ram
summary: In the ages before the Ark came to rest on Ararat, a sacred ram carried the seeds of all living things through the floodwaters, guided by the light between its horns.
full_text:
Before the Ark ground its belly upon the slopes of Ararat, before the waters withdrew to reveal a world made new, there was Shir. He was not an ordinary ram, though he looked like one from a distance. His fleece was white as the bone of the moon, and between his horns burned a light that was neither flame nor star but something older than both. The priests of the old world called him Sheed, the Luminous One, and they said he had been born from the first ray of sun that ever touched the earth.

When the Flood came and the mountains were swallowed one by one, Shir stood upon the highest ridge of the land that would one day be called Armenia. The waters rose to his knees, then his belly, then his chest. All around him the world drowned. But Shir did not drown. As the water reached his throat, he lowered his great head and breathed in, and the light between his horns blazed so bright that the waters parted around him like a curtain of glass.

Beneath his fleece, woven into the very roots of his wool, were the seeds of every plant that had ever grown upon the earth. Grain and grape, cedar and thorn, the medicinal herbs that healed the sick and the poisonous ones that killed the wicked. All of them slept in the warmth of Shir's body, waiting for the water to recede.

On the third day, Shir came to a place where the water was still and black and deep. From the depths something rose: a great serpent, black as the water itself, with eyes the colour of a sky that has never known sun. It was Vishap, the dragon of the deep, and it had survived the Flood by becoming one with the water. 'The waters are mine,' Vishap hissed. 'Whatever you carry, it belongs to the flood now.'

Shir answered not with words but with light. He lowered his head, and the light between his horns reached into the black water and found the serpent's eyes. Vishap screamed and recoiled into the depths, but it did not flee. It followed Shir for seven days and seven nights along the hidden floor of the world.

On the eighth day the water began to fall. The slopes of Ararat emerged, and Shir climbed toward the resting Ark. When he reached the summit, he shook himself, and the seeds flew from his fleece like snow. Where each seed landed, something grew. In an hour the mountain was green. In a day it bloomed with every flower that had ever existed.

Vishap, seeing this, retreated to the deepest waters, where it remains to this day, coiled in the dark, guarding its resentment. And Shir lay down upon the summit and closed his eyes. The light between his horns flickered and went out, but his body sank into the mountain and became part of it. The Armenians say that when spring comes to Ararat, the first green shoots always grow in the shape of a ram's horns.

To this day the shepherds of Armenia honor Shir. They do not shear the rams that graze upon Ararat's high pastures until the feast of Vardavar, and the first wool they take is burned as an offering. They say that every blade of grass in Armenia grew first from Shir's fleece, and that the light between his horns still sleeps deep in the mountain, waiting for the next great darkness.
themes: the bond between creature and land
moral: The smallest vessel may carry the greatest cargo; what endures the flood is not the strongest but the most faithful to its task.

title: The Dakhanavars of the Mountain Pass
summary: Two vampires haunt a remote mountain pass in Armenia, draining travelers of their blood through their feet, until a clever monk devises a trap of iron and prayer.
full_text:
There was a time when the road between the monastery of Geghard and the village of Garni was the most dangerous path in all of Armenia. Not because of bandits or wolves, but because of the Dakhanavars.

They were two, and they had no names. They had once been men, so the story goes, but they had drunk too deeply of a forbidden spring that flowed beneath the cliff face, a spring the old priests said connected to the underworld. The water changed them. It made them hungry in a way food could never satisfy, and strong in the way dead things are strong, for they did not tire and did not age.

The Dakhanavars did not attack as wolves attack. They were subtle, patient, and above all quiet. When a traveler passed through the gorge, the brothers would descend from the cliff on their bellies, clinging to the rock like lizards, and follow from above. When the traveler sat to rest, they would lower themselves upon him and feed. Not from his throat, as western vampires do, but from his feet. They pierced the soles with needle-thin fangs and drew blood slowly, gently, so that the traveler felt only a deep weariness and cold creeping upward from the ground.

By morning the traveler would be dead, or if the Dakhanavars were not hungry enough to kill, he would rise pale and weak, having lost something essential. The women said they had lost their laughter. The men said they had lost their courage.

Father Hovhannes, the abbot of Geghard, decided the Dakhanavars must be stopped. He studied the old texts and learned they could not cross running water, could not bear the smell of iron, and feared the names of the saints, not because they were holy but because the names were old and had power, and the Dakhanavars were creatures of silence that could not endure sounds they did not understand.

Father Hovhannes gathered twelve monks and gave them iron nails, each inscribed with a saint's name in letters so small only a scribe could read them. They worked through the night, hammering nails into every stone where a traveler might rest. By dawn the gorge was studded with iron.

That evening Father Hovhannes himself walked into the gorge, carrying only a lantern and a book of prayers, and sat upon the largest stone, the one the villagers called the Widow's Rest. He opened his book and began to read.

The brothers came, sliding silently down the cliff face. But when the first touched the stone, the iron screamed, or so it seemed, and the Dakhanavar recoiled as though burned. Father Hovhannes continued reading, and each word was a nail, each sentence a hammer, and the names of the saints rang through the gorge like bells.

The Dakhanavars fled, climbing the cliff in a frenzy, retreating into the deepest crevice in the rock. Father Hovhannes followed on his belly, still reading, until the brothers had burrowed so far into the mountain that no man could follow. He sealed the crevice with a wall of iron-nailed stone and marked it with a cross.

The pass was declared safe. But the monks say that on quiet nights, if you press your ear to the rock near the Widow's Rest, you can hear a faint sound from deep within the mountain, like two voices whispering in a language that has no name. The Dakhanavars have not died. They are merely waiting, patient as they have always been, for the iron to rust and the names to be forgotten.
moral: Evil that is subtle and patient requires a protector who is equally so; brute force will not overcome what whispers.

title: The Dev of the Iron Cave
summary: A giant Dev imprisoned in a cave beneath the Armenian highlands offers a miner riches beyond measure in exchange for his freedom, testing the limits of mortal greed.
full_text:
In the days when the mines of Alaverdi were still young, there was a miner named Grigor who was known throughout the province for two things: his skill with a pickaxe and his refusal to be impressed by anything. His wife said this was bravery. His mother said it was foolishness.

Grigor was digging a new shaft when his pickaxe struck something that was not stone. Instead of the dull thud of iron on rock, there was a ring, clear and deep, like a bell struck in a cathedral. The rock face cracked, and behind it was a cave, and in the cave was a Dev.

It was enormous, filling the cave the way a storm fills a valley. It had a face that was a landscape of ridges and hollows, eyes like burned-out mines and a mouth like a fissure in the earth. Its skin was the colour of raw copper, and its hair was black iron wire.

'Ah,' the Dev said, and its voice was the sound of a thousand tons of rock settling. 'A miner. How fortunate.'

'What do you want?' Grigor asked.

'Gold. I know where the veins run, Grigor. I have listened to the mountain for centuries. There is a lode beneath this cave that would make the mines of Alaverdi look like a child's treasure box. Free me, and I will tell you where it lies.'

Grigor looked at the carved seal stone in the wall behind the Dev. He reached for it, and the Dev's eyes brightened.

But Grigor stopped. He really looked at the creature, and he saw the hunger it hid behind its patience and golden promises. It was not the hunger of a man for gold. It was the hunger of fire for wood, of flood for valley. If freed, it would not reward him. It would consume everything.

'No,' Grigor said.

The Dev's patience collapsed into rage so vast the cave walls cracked. 'You dare refuse me? I will crush you.'

'Perhaps,' Grigor said, his voice steady though his hands shook. 'But I will not free you.'

He ran through the darkness, feeling his way by touch, and the mountain shook around him. He emerged into daylight and told the elders, who sealed the shaft with twelve tons of stone and a prayer.

Grigor never spoke of the gold he had refused. But sometimes late at night he would stare at his hands, trembling. His wife would say, 'You are not afraid.' And he would answer, 'No. I am not afraid. But I am aware. And awareness is a heavier burden than fear.'

The Dev remains in its cave. The priests say it will remain until the mountain crumbles. But the stone holds, and the seal holds, and the prayers of a hundred years have been layered upon the entrance like mortar upon brick. The Dev whispers, and the mountain listens, but it does not answer.
moral: The greatest treasure a man can possess is the wisdom to know when a gift is truly a chain.

title: The Vishap on the Mountain of the Ark
summary: A primordial dragon guards the deepest waters beneath Mount Ararat, dreaming of a second Flood that will return the world to the chaos it once commanded.
full_text:
The Armenians say the world was made twice. The first time, from water, and the water moved according to its own will, and the will of water is chaos. The second time, from earth and light, and the chaos was pushed down beneath the roots of the mountains, where it still churns and dreams.

The Vishap was the first thing the chaos made. It was not a creature born from other creatures, but a shape chaos gave to itself when it wanted to see and be seen. Its scales were the colour of a sky that has never known dawn, and its eyes were older than the mountain, older than the stars.

When the Flood came, the Vishap rose and rejoiced. For a time the world was as it had been: all water, all chaos, all darkness. But the waters receded, the earth emerged, and the Vishap was driven back into the deep.

It has never forgiven the earth.

Beneath Ararat, in a cavern no mine has ever reached, the Vishap waits and dreams. In its dreams the water rises again. The earth sinks. The mountains drown. And the Vishap swims free, master of a world with no form and no law.

The shepherds of Ararat know the Vishap is there. They feel it in the ground's trembling on still nights, in streams that run cold under hot sun, in caves that exhale salt air though the sea is a hundred miles away. They leave offerings at the mountain's base: bowls of milk, dried herbs, clay dragons broken upon the stone to send the Vishap's image back into the earth.

There was a time when a king of Armenia tried to slay the Vishap. He gathered his bravest warriors and miners and led them to the cave where the dragon's breath was strongest. They dug for seven days past copper veins and iron seams, past underground rivers and caverns where blind fish swam in liquid stone.

On the eighth day the Vishap found them. A sound rose from the deepest point, so low it was felt rather than heard, a vibration that turned men's bones to water. The earth opened. The miners screamed and ran, but the king stood his ground.

The Vishap did not emerge. A wind came from the crevice, cold and wet and smelling of the deep sea, and where it touched the king's skin, the skin turned grey and then black and then transparent, showing the bone beneath. The king fled and died three days later, his body cold, his eyes the colour of deep water.

Since that day no one has tried to find the Vishap. The cave has been sealed with stones and prayers. But the Armenians say that as long as there are those who remember Shir the Holy Ram, who carried the seeds of all growing things through the first Flood, the Vishap cannot rise. For Shir left a light in the mountain, buried deeper than the Vishap's cavern, a promise that the world will not be taken by water again. The Vishap dreams of the Flood, but the light of Shir dreams of the spring, and between those dreams the mountain holds, and the earth endures.
themes: the balance between destruction and renewal
moral: The forces of chaos are never truly vanquished, only held in balance by the sacred promises woven into the foundations of the world.
